details:
**Paradise Lost**
Milton's blank-verse epic (1667, revised into 12 books in 1674) retelling the fall of Satan and the temptation and fall of Adam and Eve, ending with their expulsion from the Garden of Eden. Milton was completely blind when he composed it and dictated it to helpers. It is the near-universal giveaway, and it is often credited with reviving blank verse in English after Shakespeare.

**"Better to reign in Hell, than serve in Heaven"**
Satan's defiant declaration in Book 1 of Paradise Lost, spoken to Beelzebub after the rebel angels are cast into Hell. In the same speech Satan says "The mind is its own place, and in itself / Can make a Heav'n of Hell, a Hell of Heav'n," and he cries "Hail horrors, hail / Infernal world." His charisma has led many readers to see him as the poem's most compelling figure.

**"Of Man's first disobedience, and the fruit / Of that forbidden tree"**
The opening line of Paradise Lost. The invocation calls on the "Heav'nly Muse, that on the secret top / Of Oreb, or of Sinai" inspired Moses (later identified with Urania), and describes the Spirit that "Dove-like sat'st brooding on the vast Abyss / And mad'st it pregnant." The narrator states his goal: to "justify the ways of God to men."

**Pandemonium**
The capital of Hell in Paradise Lost, built in Book 1 by the fallen angels under the architect Mulciber. In Book 2, Satan, Beelzebub, Mammon, Moloch, and Belial hold a council there and decide to corrupt God's new creation, mankind. Milton coined the word, meaning "all the demons."

**Other Paradise Lost episodes and characters**
Satan and Beelzebub first appear lying on a burning lake that gives off "darkness visible." Satan disguises himself as a cherub to trick the archangel Uriel, guardian of the Sun, into pointing the way to Eden; the archangel Raphael is sent to warn Adam; and the newly created Eve falls in love with her own reflection in a pool. An undergraduate discovered the acrostic "FFAALLAF," which spells "fall" in both directions, hidden in Book 9, the book of the Fall.

**"hand in hand, with wand'ring steps and slow, / Through Eden took their solitary way"**
The closing lines of Paradise Lost, describing Adam and Eve leaving Eden after the archangel Michael has shown them the future of humanity.

**Sonnet 19, "When I consider how my light is spent" ("On His Blindness")**
Milton's sonnet on going blind, asking "Doth God exact day-labour, light denied?" Patience answers that God does not need man's work and ends the poem with "They also serve who only stand and wait." Other sonnets in clues include Sonnet 23, "Methought I saw my late espoused Saint," a dream vision of his dead wife, and Sonnet 7, which laments how little he has achieved by age twenty-three.

**"Lycidas"**
Milton's 1637 pastoral elegy for Edward King, a Cambridge classmate who drowned in the Irish Sea. It opens "Yet once more, O ye laurels" (the speaker comes "to pluck your berries harsh and crude"), calls on the "Sisters of the sacred well," features St. Peter as "the Pilot of the Galilean lake" with a mysterious "two-handed engine," and urges "Look homeward, Angel, now, and melt with ruth." The "uncouth swain" ends by telling the "woeful shepherds" to "weep no more."

**"Il Penseroso"**
"The Thoughtful Man," a poem that opens "Hence, vain deluding Joys, / The brood of Folly" and praises "divinest Melancholy," daughter of Vesta and Saturn. The speaker seeks twilight groves, study, and wishes to "unsphere / The spirit of Plato," and ends "These pleasures Melancholy give, / And I with thee will choose to live."

**"L'Allegro"**
"The Cheerful Man," the companion poem to "Il Penseroso." It opens "Hence, loathed Melancholy, / Of Cerberus and blackest Midnight born," invites Mirth with "Jest, and youthful Jollity," asks to be lapped "in soft Lydian airs, / Married to immortal verse," and ends "Mirth, with thee I mean to live."

**Areopagitica**
Milton's 1644 prose tract against Parliament's Licensing Order of 1643, which required books to be approved before printing. Titled after the Areopagus hill in Athens and opening with an epigraph from Euripides on "true liberty," it argues that "he who destroys a good book, kills reason itself" and praises the Christian who knows vice yet prefers what is truly better. It followed the controversy over his divorce tracts, including The Doctrine and Discipline of Divorce, Tetrachordon, and Colasterion.

**Samson Agonistes**
Milton's closet drama (1671) about the biblical Samson, now blind, shorn, and a prisoner of the Philistines, "Eyeless in Gaza." He resists his wife Dalila and the giant Harapha before pulling down the Philistine temple. It ends with "calm of mind, all passion spent," and its "Eyeless in Gaza" gave Aldous Huxley a novel title.

**Paradise Regained**
Milton's four-book "brief epic," published with Samson Agonistes in 1671, in which Christ resists Satan's temptations in the wilderness. It was inspired by the Quaker Thomas Ellwood, who, after reading Paradise Lost, asked Milton what he had to say about "Paradise found."

**"Malt does more than Milton can / To justify God's ways to man"**
Lines from A. E. Housman's "Terence, this is stupid stuff" in A Shropshire Lad, joking that beer consoles better than Paradise Lost's stated purpose.

**Milton in other writers' poems**
William Blake's epic Milton: A Poem contains the preface lyric "And did those feet in ancient time" and has Milton's spirit enter Blake's foot. Wordsworth's "London, 1802" opens "Milton! thou shouldst be living at this hour" and praises his "cheerful godliness." Thomas Gray's "Elegy Written in a Country Churchyard" imagines that "Some mute inglorious Milton here may rest."
